newsitem.title: GERMANY: Cohen carries tough Bosnia message to Europe.
newsitem.headline: Cohen carries tough Bosnia message to Europe.

text.p: New U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen warned on Tuesday that American troops would leave Bosnia for good in mid-1998 even if peace crumbled and Serbs, Moslems and Croats went back to war.

"I can't make it any clearer ," Cohen told reporters flying with him from Washington to Bonn for talks with Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Defence Minister Volker Ruehe and a four-day trip to Germany, Bosnia, Italy and NATO headquarters in Brussels.

"If they (Bosnians) choose not to pursue peace, that is going to be their choice. But if you accept the argument that if they are at each other's throats that we stay longer, we will be there for decades," he said, repeating warnings issued during his first month as Defence Secretary.

"So it is very clear that in June of 1998 we will be on our way out," Cohen said. "The parties will have to make that determination ... is that (peace) something they wish to pursue or do they want to go back to slaughtering each other?"
Cohen was holding talks with Ruehe later on Tuesday before meeting Kohl on Wednesday on his first overseas trip since replacing Defence Secretary William Perry.

Later this week, he will visit some of the nearly 8,000 U.S. peacekeeping troops in Bosnia, then go to Rome for talks with Italian Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta and to Brussels for meetings with NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana and permanent representatives to the alliance.

Some European officials are already suggesting that a new Bosnia peace force, perhaps headed by the European Union, might be needed when the current NATO-led stabilisation force (SFOR) of 31,000 troops leaves Bosnia in mid-1998.

But Cohen said the United States would not provide any ground troops for such a force because Washington was already spending some $6.5 billion on its peacekeeping contingent there and had other military budget and security problems to face.

"As I have indicated before, I still believe it is primarily a European problem to deal with. It was not dealt with by the Europeans and the United States became engaged only frankly as a last resort when it saw the commission of so many atrocities," the secretary said.
He rejected the notion that peacekeeping in Bosnia would work only if U.S. troops were part of the mix.

"This is a region in which the ethnic rivalries and hatreds run very deep and if we accept that premise -- that peace will be only be secure so long as he United States is involved -- it means that we would make almost a semi-permanent commitment to be there.
"I don't think the American people will support that. I know that Congress won't support it, I don't think the President is going to recommend it."
Cohen, 56, a former senator from Maine, is the only Republican on President Bill Clinton's Cabinet and has emphasised since taking office that the United States cannot be the world's peacekeeper.

Cohen said the United States and France were still discussing Washington's refusal to bow to a French demand that the U.S. military turn the command of southern NATO forces based in Naples to a European officer.
He said he agreed with French pressure to settle the dispute by May but that "there has been no change to my knowledge in the position that AFSOUTH (allied forces south) remain under U.S. control."
France earlier indicated that it was prepared to rejoin the NATO military structure after an absence of over 30 years, but that step has been held up by the dispute.
